newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish pound steadies while digesting rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Irish pound steadies while digesting rate rise.

text.p: The Irish pound steadied at 0.9200/50 stg towards the close of business on Thursday following a surprise half point interest rate rise by Ireland's central bank.
The punt, which had hit a five-year low against sterling on Wednesday after a sharp sell-off, stopped in its tracks to digest what some economists called 'a statement of intent' by the central bank.
The Irish pound dropped 6.5 pfennigs against the mark on Wednesday after Ireland's central bank indicated it was not going to intervene to shore up the ailing currency late on Tuesday.

The punt encountered huge selling pressure on the assumption that Ireland would have to drop to the central rate within the European Exchange Rate Mechanism if it hoped to enter a single currency in 1999. This would imply a level of 2.41 against the mark, dealers said.
The punt continued to slide on Thursday but steadied after a surprise announcement that the central bank was raising the official Short Term Facility (STF) rate by half a point to 6.75 percent.
By 1709 GMT, the punt was quoted at 0.9200/50 from 0.9135 before the rate rise. It closed on Wednesday at 0.9248 stg.
It was at 2.5623/38 marks after the announcement, up from 2.5615 marks before the central bank move but still well off Wednesday's close of 2.5992.
One-month interbank rates were quoted at 6.75/7.00 percent after the announcement.

"Cash is still trading well above the STF," Riada economist Dan McLaughlin said. "In 1995, in similar circumstances, the central bank raised the STF by half a point in one week and another half a point the next."

"Rates are still not high enough to dissuade people from selling the punt but obviously this is done mainly to tighten domestic policy and we should see a half point rise in mortgage rates," McLaughlin said.
